outcome: I can use a PPC to explain scarcity, choice, opportunity cost, unemployment of resources and economic growth.

learn.text:
Every economy faces [[scarcity]]: resources are limited, so it must choose what to produce. A [[production possibilities curve|PPC]] shows the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can make when it uses all its resources fully and efficiently, with given technology.

Points on the curve are efficient. A point inside the curve means [[unemployment of resources|unemployed resources]], and a point outside cannot be reached yet. Moving along the curve shows [[opportunity cost]]: to make more of one good, you give up some of the other.

When resources are not equally good at making both goods, the PPC bows outward and shows [[increasing opportunity cost]]. More or better resources, or new technology, shift the PPC outward. This is [[growth in production possibilities]]. Using unemployed resources moves the economy from inside towards the curve. This is [[actual growth]].
learn.caption: A is on the PPC (efficient). B is inside (unemployed resources). C is outside (unattainable for now). The arrow shows growth in production possibilities: PPC₁ shifts out to PPC₂.

try.intro:
**Welcome to Pinewood Island**. Ten islanders can catch fish or cut timber. Some are great at fishing, some are great at cutting timber.

**Four seasons:** plan the island's year. Each season has three steps. 1. **Predict** what the event does to the PPC. 2. **Put each islander in a job** so the island meets the season's need. 3. Answer a short **opportunity cost** question. Each right prediction and each right answer earns a star. There are three levels. Each one opens when you earn the stamp for the level before.

**Missions:** six short tasks, one at a time. Each mission tells you what to do and how to do it. They teach the controls and the key ideas. Then try the event scenarios: predict before you play each scenario.

missions.text: Produce **on** the PPC with at least 30 tonnes of fish.
missions.title: Use every worker well
how: Check that **Workers with jobs** shows 10 of 10.
Use **−** and **+** next to **Workers fishing** to move workers.
Stop when **Position** says **On the PPC** and **Fish** is 30 tonnes or more.
missions.done: Every worker has a job and the island makes as much as it can. That is **productive efficiency**: a point **on** the PPC.

missions.text: Show **unemployment of resources**: make the island produce at a point **inside** the PPC.
missions.title: Show unemployment
how: Move it to the left so some workers have no job.
Watch the red dot move **inside** the PPC.
missions.done: Some workers have no job, so the island makes less than it could. A point **inside** the PPC shows **unemployment of resources**.

missions.text: Tap the diagram to find a point **outside** the PPC. Why can the island not produce there?
missions.title: Find an impossible point
how: Tap or click the diagram **above and to the right** of the curve.
A label appears to say if your point is inside, on or outside the PPC.
missions.done: The island cannot make this much with its workers and technology. Points **outside** the PPC are **unattainable** today. Only **growth in production possibilities** (more or better resources, or better technology) could reach them.

missions.text: With every worker employed, move one worker into fishing where each extra fish costs **more than 2 tonnes** of timber.
missions.title: Watch the cost rise
how: Check that **Increasing opportunity cost** is on and **Workers with jobs** shows 10 of 10.
Press **+** next to **Workers fishing** one worker at a time.
Read the **Opportunity cost counter** after each move. Keep going until one extra tonne of fish costs **more than 2** tonnes of timber.
missions.done: The last workers to move are great at timber and poor at fishing. So each extra tonne of fish costs more timber. This is **increasing opportunity cost**, and it makes the PPC bow outward.

missions.text: Switch to **constant opportunity cost** and compare the shape of the PPC.
missions.title: Compare a straight PPC
how: Look at the new shape of the PPC.
Move workers with **+** and look at the opportunity cost bars.
missions.done: Now every worker is equally good at both jobs. Each extra tonne of fish always costs the same timber, so the PPC is a **straight line**.

missions.text: Predict and play at least one **event scenario**.
missions.title: Predict an event
how: Read it and choose what you think it will do to the PPC.
Click **See what happens** to see if you were right.
missions.done: Events can **shift** the PPC (resources or technology change) or **move** the island inside or back onto it (jobs change). Try the other scenarios too.

outcomes.text: The PPC pivots out along the fish axis only
The PPC pivots in along the fish axis only
The PPC pivots out along the timber axis only
The PPC pivots in along the timber axis only
The island moves to a point inside the PPC
The island moves from inside towards the PPC

events.title: New families arrive
events.text: Two new families move to the island, adding 2 workers who are average at both jobs.
events.explain: More labour means the island can make more of both goods. The whole PPC shifts outward. This is growth in production possibilities.

events.title: Sawmill closes
events.text: The island's sawmill closes for repairs, and 3 workers lose their jobs. The workers and their skills are still on the island.
events.explain: The island still has the same resources and technology, so the PPC does not move. But some workers are unemployed, so the island produces at a point inside the PPC. Inside the curve means unemployment of resources.

events.title: Sawmill reopens
events.text: The sawmill reopens and hires back unemployed workers.
events.explain: Putting unemployed workers back to work increases output without any change in resources or technology. The point moves from inside the PPC towards the curve. This is actual growth. The PPC itself does not shift.

events.title: A cyclone
events.text: A cyclone wrecks boats and blows down part of the forest. Every worker can now catch 30% fewer fish and cut 30% less timber.
events.explain: A natural disaster that destroys resources used for both goods reduces what the island can produce. The **whole PPC shifts inward**.

events.title: New fishing nets
events.text: A local firm invents a stronger, lighter fishing net. Every worker can now catch 50% more fish. Timber cutting does not change.
events.explain: Better technology in fishing lets the island make more fish with the same workers, but no more timber. The PPC pivots outward along the fish axis. The timber end stays where it was. This is growth in production possibilities for fish.

seasonLevels.title: A calm year
seasonLevels.blurb: Put each islander in the right job. Events shift the whole PPC or change the number of jobs. Earn 5 of 7 stars.

seasons.name: Spring
seasons.story: Last year's council put many islanders in the wrong jobs. Look at what each islander is good at, then move them. The island needs wood to repair homes and fish to eat.

check.q: Dara can catch 7 tonnes of fish **or** cut 4 tonnes of timber. Dara moves from timber to fishing. What is the opportunity cost of **each tonne of fish** Dara catches?
check.explain: Dara gives up 4 tonnes of timber to catch 7 tonnes of fish. So each tonne of fish costs 4 ÷ 7 = **0.57 tonnes of timber**. Opportunity cost = what you give up ÷ what you gain.

seasons.name: Summer
seasons.story: Summer visitors arrive and want to eat fish. The island also needs timber for new jetties.

event.title: A new harbour and better tools
event.text: The island builds a new harbour and buys better tools. Every islander can now catch 30% more fish **and** cut 30% more timber.
event.explain: Better capital helps both jobs, so the island can make more of both goods. The **whole PPC shifts outward**. This is growth in production possibilities.

check.q: After the new harbour and tools, Dara can catch 9.1 tonnes of fish or cut 5.2 tonnes of timber. What happened to the opportunity cost of Dara's fish?
choices: It stayed the same: 0.57 tonnes of timber
check.explain: Both jobs became 30% more productive, so 5.2 ÷ 9.1 is still **0.57**. When output of both goods grows by the same percentage, the opportunity cost does not change. The whole PPC shifts out.

seasons.name: Autumn
seasons.story: The island stores food for winter and stacks firewood. With fewer jobs, think about **who** should stay at home.

event.title: Sawmill closes
event.text: The sawmill closes for repairs. 3 jobs are lost, so only 7 islanders can work. The council chooses who.
event.explain: Resources and technology do not change, so the PPC stays where it is. With 3 islanders unemployed, the island can only produce at a point **inside** the PPC.

check.q: Each tonne of Ana's fish costs 0.1 tonnes of timber. Each tonne of Hana's fish costs 2.67 tonnes of timber. What does this show?
choices: Increasing opportunity cost: the more fish the island makes, the more timber each extra tonne costs
Constant opportunity cost: every tonne of fish costs the same
Hana does not work as hard as Ana
Fish are worth more than timber
check.explain: The first islanders to fish are good at it, so fish is cheap. Later islanders are better at timber, so each extra tonne of fish costs more timber. This is **increasing opportunity cost**, and it makes the PPC bow outward.

seasons.name: Winter
seasons.story: It is cold. The island needs firewood to stay warm and fish to stay fed.

event.title: Sawmill reopens
event.text: The sawmill reopens. The 3 lost jobs come back.
event.explain: Nothing about the island's resources or technology changed, so the PPC does not move. Putting unemployed islanders back to work moves the island from inside the PPC **towards** the curve. This is actual growth.

check.q: Why does Pinewood Island's PPC bow outward (concave to the origin)?
choices: Fishing is harder than cutting timber
The islanders have different skills, so moving more of them into fishing costs more and more timber per tonne of fish
check.explain: Resources are **not equally suited** to both jobs. Each extra tonne of fish needs an islander who is worse at fishing and better at timber, so the opportunity cost rises. Rising opportunity cost gives a bowed PPC.

seasonLevels.title: A stormy year
seasonLevels.blurb: Tighter needs: only a few plans work. Four events and four cost questions, including constant opportunity cost. Earn 6 of 8 stars.

seasons.name: Spring
seasons.story: The islanders want to build a new school, so they need a lot of timber, and fish too.

event.title: The island trains its workers
event.text: A new training course teaches every islander better methods. Each islander can catch 20% more fish and cut 20% more timber.
event.explain: Better human capital raises output of both goods. The **whole PPC shifts outward**: the island can now produce more of both.

check.q: On **Flat Rock**, the island next door, every worker can catch 6 tonnes of fish or cut 6 tonnes of timber. What does Flat Rock's PPC look like?
choices: A straight line: each tonne of fish always costs 1 tonne of timber
check.explain: On Flat Rock every worker is **equally good** at both jobs. Moving any worker gives up 6 timber for 6 fish, so each tonne of fish always costs 1 tonne of timber. **Constant opportunity cost** gives a straight-line PPC.

seasons.name: Summer
seasons.story: Visitors arrive. The island needs fish for them and timber for the school. With two islanders sick, think about **who** stays home.

event.title: A summer fever
event.text: A fever goes round the island. Two islanders are too sick to work all summer.
event.explain: The island's resources and technology have not changed, so the PPC stays where it is. Two islanders are not producing, so the island can only reach a point **inside** the PPC.

check.q: After training, Ana can catch 12 tonnes of fish or cut 1.2 tonnes of timber. Gus can catch 4.8 tonnes of fish or cut 8.4 tonnes of timber. Who should fish, and why?
choices: Ana: each tonne of her fish costs only 0.1 tonnes of timber, but each tonne of Gus's costs 1.75
Gus: he can cut more timber, so he is the better worker
It makes no difference who fishes
Neither: they should both cut timber
check.explain: Put each islander where their opportunity cost is lowest. Ana gives up 1.2 ÷ 12 = **0.1 tonnes of timber** per tonne of fish. Gus gives up 8.4 ÷ 4.8 = **1.75 tonnes**. Ana fishing and Gus cutting timber gets the most from both.

seasons.name: Autumn
seasons.story: The island stores food and wood before the cold weather. Everything must be just right.

event.title: Everyone recovers
event.text: The two sick islanders are well again and can go back to work.
event.explain: Nothing about the island's resources or technology has changed, so the PPC does not move. The islanders who come back move the island from inside the PPC **towards** the curve.

check.q: With every islander working, the island moves from 4 islanders fishing (40.8 fish, 54 timber) to 5 fishing (48 fish, 48 timber). What is the opportunity cost of **each extra tonne of fish**?
check.explain: The island gains 48 − 40.8 = 7.2 tonnes of fish and gives up 54 − 48 = 6 tonnes of timber. Each tonne of fish costs 6 ÷ 7.2 = **0.83 tonnes of timber**.

seasons.name: Winter
seasons.story: A long winter. The island needs firewood and fish in equal amounts.

event.title: A great storm
event.text: A storm wrecks boats and blows down part of the forest. Every islander can now catch 20% fewer fish and cut 20% less timber.
event.explain: Resources used for both goods are destroyed, so the island can make less of both. The **whole PPC shifts inward**.

check.q: Which change would turn Pinewood's bowed PPC into a **straight line**?
choices: More islanders move to the island
Every islander becomes equally good at fishing and cutting timber
Everyone who wants a job has one
check.explain: A straight-line PPC needs **constant opportunity cost**. That happens when every resource is equally suited to both goods, like the workers on Flat Rock. More islanders or better tools shift the curve but keep its bowed shape.

seasonLevels.title: The council's year
seasonLevels.blurb: Some events change only one good, the islanders are mixed up, and one need cannot be met at all. Spot it. Earn 7 of 8 stars.

seasons.name: Spring
seasons.story: The island must repair homes and still feed everyone. Read each islander's skills: the list is mixed up this year.

event.title: Half the reef is closed
event.text: To protect young fish, the council closes half the reef. Every islander can now catch only 60% as many fish. Timber does not change.
event.explain: Fewer fishing grounds is a loss of a resource used only for fish. The fish end of the PPC moves in and the timber end stays. The PPC **pivots inward along the fish axis**.

check.q: After the reef closes, Ana can catch 6 tonnes of fish or cut 1 tonne of timber. What is the opportunity cost of **each tonne of fish** Ana catches?
choices: 0.1 tonnes of timber, the same as before
check.explain: Ana gives up 1 tonne of timber for 6 tonnes of fish, so each tonne of fish costs 1 ÷ 6 = **0.17 tonnes of timber**. Before the reef closed it was 1 ÷ 10 = 0.1. Fish became harder to catch, so each tonne costs more timber.

seasons.name: Summer
seasons.story: The council asks for a lot of fish and even more timber. Can the island do it?

event.title: Sharper saw blades
event.text: A new saw blade lets every islander cut 30% more timber. Fishing does not change.
event.explain: Better technology for timber only lets the island make more timber with the same islanders, but no more fish. The PPC **pivots outward along the timber axis**.

check.q: **Island A** can make 0, 10, 20 or 30 tonnes of fish, with 30, 20, 10 or 0 tonnes of timber. **Island B** can make 0, 10, 20 or 30 tonnes of fish, with 30, 27, 20 or 0 tonnes of timber. Which island has **constant** opportunity cost?
choices: Island B: each tonne of fish always costs 1 tonne of timber
Island A: each tonne of fish always costs 1 tonne of timber
check.explain: On Island A, every 10 extra tonnes of fish costs 10 tonnes of timber: always **1 tonne each**, so its PPC is a straight line. On Island B the cost rises from 0.3 to 0.7 to 2 tonnes: increasing opportunity cost, a bowed PPC.

seasons.name: Autumn
seasons.story: With fewer islanders working, the island needs just enough to get by. Choose who works with care.

event.title: A harbour strike
event.text: Four islanders go on strike and stop working. Only 6 jobs are filled.
event.explain: The island still has the same resources and technology, so the PPC does not move. With four islanders not working, the island produces at a point **inside** the PPC.

check.q: The island is inside its PPC because 4 islanders are on strike. If they go back to work, what must the island give up?
choices: Some timber, to make more fish
Some fish, to make more timber
Nothing: it can make more fish **and** more timber
check.explain: Inside the PPC, resources are unemployed. Putting them to work raises output of both goods, so there is **no opportunity cost** of moving towards the curve. Opportunity cost appears when you move **along** the PPC.

seasons.name: Winter
seasons.story: The coldest season. Every tonne counts.

event.title: The strike ends
event.text: The four islanders return to work.
event.explain: The PPC stays where it is, because resources and technology are the same. Returning islanders move the island from inside the PPC back **towards** the curve.

check.q: Pinewood's PPC is bowed. Flat Rock's PPC is a straight line. On which island does the **last** worker moved into fishing cost the most timber for each tonne of fish?
choices: Pinewood: its last fisher is its best timber cutter
check.explain: On Pinewood, the last islander to move into fishing is Jaya, the best at timber and the worst at fishing. Each tonne of Jaya's fish costs a lot of timber. On Flat Rock every worker costs the same. Increasing versus constant opportunity cost.

try.goal: Plan Pinewood Island's year in **Four seasons**. New to PPCs? Start with **Missions**: six short tasks, one at a time.

check.prompt: An economy produces at a point **inside** its PPC. What does this show?

options.text: Unemployment of resources
options.feedback: Yes. Some resources are not being used, so output is less than the economy could make.

options.text: The economy is efficient
options.feedback: Efficient points are **on** the curve, where all resources are fully used. A point inside is below the maximum.

options.text: The combination cannot be produced
options.feedback: That describes a point **outside** the PPC. A point inside can be produced; it is just less than the maximum.

options.text: Growth in production possibilities
options.feedback: Growth in production possibilities is shown by the whole PPC shifting outward, not by a point inside it.

hints: Think about what is different between a point on the curve and a point below it.
Points on the curve use all resources fully. What is happening to some resources at a point below?
check.worked: Example: Pinewood Island can make 55 tonnes of timber with all 10 workers. It makes only 40 tonnes because 3 workers have no job. Output is inside the PPC because resources (labour) are unemployed.
check.explanation: A point inside the PPC means the economy is not using all its resources, or not using them efficiently. Output could rise with no new resources, just by employing the idle ones.

check.prompt: Why does a PPC usually **bow outward** (concave to the origin)?

options.text: Resources are not equally suited to making both goods, so opportunity cost increases
options.feedback: Yes. Moving more resources into one good means using resources that are worse at it, so each extra unit costs more of the other good.

options.text: Opportunity cost is the same for every unit
options.feedback: Constant opportunity cost gives a **straight-line** PPC, not a bowed one.

options.text: The economy has unemployed resources
options.feedback: Unemployment shows as a point inside the PPC. It does not change the curve's shape.

options.text: Technology improves over time
options.feedback: Better technology shifts the PPC outward. It does not explain why the curve bows.

hints: Remember the bars in the opportunity cost counter. What happened to them as you moved more workers into fishing?
Were all ten workers equally good at fishing?
check.worked: On Pinewood Island the first worker moved into fishing gave up 1 tonne of timber for 10 tonnes of fish (0.1 timber per fish). The last worker gave up 10 tonnes of timber for just 1 tonne of fish (10 timber per fish). The cost of fish rises, so the curve bows outward.
check.explanation: The PPC bows outward because of increasing opportunity cost. Resources are specialised, so the first units of a good use the resources best at making it, and later units use resources better suited to the other good.

check.prompt: Use the PPC schedule. The economy moves from point B to point C. What is the **opportunity cost of each extra unit of capital goods**, in consumer goods?

mistakes.feedback: 20 is the total consumer goods given up. Divide by the 10 extra capital goods to find the cost of **each** one.
That is capital goods per consumer good. The question asks how many **consumer goods** are given up per extra capital good.
70 is the amount of consumer goods made at C, not the amount given up.

hints: Opportunity cost = what you give up ÷ what you gain.
From B to C, consumer goods fall from 90 to 70, and capital goods rise from 10 to 20.
check.worked: Example with different points: from A to B, consumer goods fall by 100 − 90 = 10 and capital goods rise by 10 − 0 = 10. Opportunity cost = 10 ÷ 10 = 1 consumer good per capital good.
check.explanation: From B to C: consumer goods given up = 90 − 70 = 20. Capital goods gained = 20 − 10 = 10. Opportunity cost = 20 ÷ 10 = **2 consumer goods** per extra capital good.

check.prompt: A country with high unemployment creates jobs for idle workers. Resources and technology do not change. How is this shown on a PPC diagram?

options.text: A movement from a point inside the PPC towards the curve (actual growth)
options.feedback: Yes. Output rises because idle resources are used, but the maximum the economy can make has not changed.

options.text: An outward shift of the PPC
options.feedback: An outward shift needs more or better resources or technology. Here those did not change.

options.text: A movement along the PPC
options.feedback: A movement along the curve shows reallocating fully employed resources between goods, not using idle resources.

options.text: An inward shift of the PPC
options.feedback: An inward shift means the economy lost resources, for example from a disaster.

hints: Did the economy's resources or technology change?
If the PPC did not move, what moved?
check.worked: Example: after the Pinewood sawmill reopened, 3 workers went back to work. Fish and timber output rose, but the PPC stayed in the same place. The island's point moved from inside towards the curve.
check.explanation: Using unemployed resources is **actual growth**: a movement from inside the PPC towards it. The PPC only shifts outward when the quantity or quality of resources rises or technology improves.

check.prompt: A country can produce robots and wheat. A new robot-making technology is invented. Farming does not change. Which diagram describes the change?

options.text: The PPC pivots outward along the robot axis; the wheat end stays the same
options.feedback: Yes. The country can make more robots with the same resources, but the most wheat it can make has not changed.

options.text: The whole PPC shifts outward equally
options.feedback: An equal outward shift would need better resources for **both** goods. Only robot technology improved.

options.text: The country moves along its PPC towards robots
options.feedback: A movement along the curve is a choice to reallocate resources. New technology changes the curve itself.

options.text: Nothing changes until the country chooses to make more robots
options.feedback: The PPC shows what is **possible**. New technology changes what is possible, even before anyone changes what they make.

hints: Ask: which maximum changes, the most robots or the most wheat?
If every resource went to wheat, would the country make more wheat than before?
check.worked: Example: on Pinewood Island, new fishing nets raised fish output by 50%. If every worker fished, the island could make more fish. If every worker cut timber, timber output was the same. So only the fish end of the PPC moved out.
check.explanation: New technology for one good raises the maximum of that good only. The PPC pivots outward from the other good's axis. This is growth in production possibilities, mainly for robots.

check.prompt: A government must choose between building more hospitals (capital goods) and producing more consumer goods today. Which statement uses the PPC model correctly?

options.text: Choosing more capital goods now means fewer consumer goods today, but it can shift the PPC outward in the future
options.feedback: Yes. The opportunity cost today is consumer goods, but more capital raises the economy's future productive capacity.

options.text: More capital goods have no opportunity cost because they help the economy grow
options.feedback: Every choice on the PPC has an opportunity cost. On the curve, more capital goods means fewer consumer goods **now**.

options.text: Producing more capital goods moves the economy inside the PPC
options.feedback: If resources stay fully employed, the economy moves **along** the curve, not inside it.

options.text: The PPC shifts outward as soon as the hospitals are chosen
options.feedback: The choice itself is a movement along today's PPC. The outward shift comes later, once the new capital adds to productive capacity.

hints: Separate what happens today from what may happen in the future.
Today: is the economy moving along the curve or shifting it? Later: what do more capital goods do to productive capacity?
check.worked: Example: a ski hill spends this year building a new chairlift instead of running more lessons. This year it gives up lesson income (opportunity cost). Next year the chairlift lets it serve more skiers, so its possibilities grow.
check.explanation: Today the choice is a movement along the PPC with an opportunity cost in consumer goods. Because capital goods increase future productive capacity, the PPC can shift outward later. This is the trade-off between consumption now and growth in the future.

check.prompt: **Label the diagram.** Choose what each lettered point shows.

diagram.title: A production possibilities curve with three lettered points
diagram.description: A curved PPC bowed out from the origin. Point A is on the curve. Point B is inside the curve. Point C is outside the curve.

slots.answer: Productively efficient: all resources fully used
slots.feedback: A is on the PPC. Every point on the curve uses all resources fully and efficiently.
B is inside the PPC. The economy could make more of both goods, so some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently.

slots.answer: Not possible with current resources and technology
slots.feedback: C is outside the PPC. The economy cannot reach it until it has more resources or better technology.

choices: Productively efficient: all resources fully used
Not possible with current resources and technology
hints: Is each point on the curve, inside it, or outside it?
On the curve = all resources used. Inside = some resources unused. Outside = cannot be reached yet.
check.worked: Example: a farm can grow 100 tonnes of wheat or 50 tonnes of corn, or combinations on its PPC. If it grows 40 wheat and 20 corn while that combination is inside the curve, some land or workers are idle. A combination outside the curve needs more land, workers or better technology.
check.explanation: A point **on** the PPC shows productive efficiency: all resources are fully used. A point **inside** shows unemployed or inefficiently used resources. A point **outside** cannot be produced now. It needs more resources or better technology (economic growth).

check.prompt: The PPC moves from PPC₁ to PPC₂. Which event could cause this?

diagram.title: Two production possibilities curves
diagram.description: PPC₁ is bowed out from the origin. PPC₂ is further from the origin at every point, so both maximum outputs are higher. An arrow points from PPC₁ to PPC₂.

options.text: More workers join the labour force, and new technology helps make both goods
options.feedback: Yes. More resources and better technology raise the maximum output of both goods, so the whole PPC shifts outward.

options.text: Unemployed workers find jobs
options.feedback: That moves the economy from a point inside the PPC towards the curve. The curve itself does not move.

options.text: People decide they want more of Good X and less of Good Y
options.feedback: A change in what people want moves the economy along the same PPC. It does not change what the economy can produce.

options.text: New technology helps make Good X only
options.feedback: Close. That would pivot the PPC outward on the Good X axis only. Here both ends have moved out.

hints: Did both ends of the PPC move, or only one?
The PPC shows what can be produced. Only a change in resources or technology moves it.
check.worked: Example: a country builds new roads and trains more workers. It can now make more of every good, so its PPC shifts outward. If only farming technology improves, only the farm-goods end moves out (a pivot).
check.explanation: An **outward shift** of the whole PPC is **economic growth** in potential output. It comes from more or better resources (labour, capital, land) or better technology that helps both goods. Fuller use of existing resources is a movement towards the curve, not a shift.

explain.prompt: Choose one event you played (for example a new harbour, the sawmill closing or a storm). Explain, using a PPC diagram, what the event did to the island.
frames: Before the event, the island could produce ___.
The event changed ___, so the PPC ___.
This means the opportunity cost of ___ changed because ___.
This is different from unemployment because ___.
checklist: I named the event and said which resource or technology changed.
I said whether the PPC shifted, pivoted, or did not move.
I explained the difference between a shift of the PPC and a point inside it.
I described a diagram with both axes labelled (fish and timber).

teacherNotes: Use projector mode and play the event scenarios as a whole-class prediction game: students show 1 to 5 fingers for the outcome before you play each scenario. In **Four seasons**, students place each islander in a job. Putting islanders in jobs that do not suit them leaves the island inside its PPC, so the game shows inefficiency as well as unemployment. Levels 1 and 2 use whole-curve shifts and changes in jobs. Level 3 adds events that change only one good (pivots). Each season ends with an opportunity cost question; Level 2 and 3 questions compare constant and increasing opportunity cost (1.1 diagram: increasing versus constant opportunity cost).
